_key_form: <file>:<RULE>:<symbol>:ast=<ast_path>, built as Finding.canonical_key with the fp= fingerprint component replaced by the module-rooted ast_path (the join key the hub's stage_annotate uses first). Symbol components are joined with ':' exactly as Finding.canonical_key does, so a method reads Class:method, never Class.method. The ast= path is load-bearing as a disambiguator in this bucket: contracts/secret_scrub.py:_scrub_value carries 4 findings, tui/screens/explain_screen.py:ExplainScreen:_add_execution_state 4, testing/__init__.py:make_success_multi 2, and tui/widgets/node_detail.py:_parse_json_object and _format_json_value 2 each, so a sidecar keyed only on (file, RULE, symbol) would silently drop 12 of the 34 rationales. All 34 keys below are unique under (file, RULE, symbol, ast_path) and were regenerated from the post-fix tree, so every one binds to the tree at this lane's final commit.
contracts/audit.py:R5:_validate_enum:ast: R5 `not isinstance(value, enum_type)` in _validate_enum. Why isinstance is right here and nothing else is: enum_type is a PARAMETER (`enum_type: type`), so the class to compare against is chosen by the caller at runtime — RunStatus, CallType, NodeType, TerminalOutcome and a dozen more. There is no static annotation that can express 'value is an instance of whatever class my caller passed', and `type(value) is enum_type` would be wrong for the IntEnum/StrEnum subclass families this codebase uses. The check is Tier-1 crash-on-corruption per the module docstring: audit enums are read back from OUR database and a string that never became an enum means the model loader failed, so it raises TypeError naming the field and the offending type rather than coercing. Same hoisted-helper mechanism as the other validators in this file: the exemption requires a literal __post_init__ frame with a self.<field> subject, and this parametric helper has neither. Invalidated if: the enum type stops being a parameter (one validator per enum class, or a generic bound), which is the only change that would make a static check possible here.
contracts/audit.py:R5:_validate_hash:ast: R5 `not isinstance(value, str)` as the first conjunct in _validate_hash, guarding _SHA256_HEX_PATTERN.fullmatch(value). Why it is right at THIS site: the isinstance is not redundant with the regex, it is a precondition FOR it — re.Pattern.fullmatch raises `TypeError: expected string or bytes-like object` on an int or None, so without the conjunct a corrupt audit hash surfaces as an opaque regex crash instead of the field-named ValueError this helper exists to raise. Short-circuit order is therefore load-bearing and the two conjuncts cannot be swapped. The value is Tier-1: a digest column read back from our own audit DB. Hoisted out of __post_init__ for reuse across many audit dataclass fields, which is why the rule's frozen-dataclass __post_init__ exemption does not see it. Invalidated if: the digest columns are given a NewType/owned Digest type constructed at the DB read boundary, so callers can no longer hand this helper a non-str at all.
contracts/audit.py:R5:_validate_nonempty: R5 `not isinstance(value, str)` as the first conjunct in _validate_nonempty_string, guarding `not value.strip()`. Same precondition role as _validate_hash but for a different failure: .strip() on an int raises AttributeError, and the point of this helper (per its docstring, 'without silently trimming them') is that a whitespace-only audit identifier is REJECTED rather than normalised to empty — so the emptiness test must run on a value already known to be str. This is the required-identifier guard for Tier-1 audit rows (run_id, node_id, token_id and friends): an identifier that is None or ' ' means the writer lost it, and a silently-accepted blank identifier makes the audit trail unjoinable. Hoisted to module scope for reuse, which is why the __post_init__ exemption misses it. Invalidated if: the identifier fields move to an owned non-empty-string type validated once at construction, removing the need for a per-field runtime guard.
contracts/audit.py:R5:validate_resolved_: R5 `not isinstance(resolved_prompt_template_hash, str)` in the module-level validator validate_resolved_prompt_template_hash. Why the exemption misses it: the tier-model rule exempts isinstance only inside a function literally named __post_init__ on a frozen dataclass, whose subject resolves to self.<field> or an alias assigned from one earlier in that same __post_init__ (_is_tier1_frozen_dataclass_post_init_guard / _post_init_self_field_aliases_before). This guard IS that check — Call.__post_init__ calls it — but it is hoisted to module scope on purpose, because the docstring makes it the single source of truth for an invariant enforced from two places: the dataclass (Call.__post_init__, audit.py:564) AND the ExecutionRepository write path (core/landscape/execution/calls.py:428 and :541), which must reject a bad hash BEFORE the audit row is inserted. Inside the frozen-dataclass frame the exemption would have applied; the hoist is what defeats the frame test, not any weakness in the check. Why isinstance is right here: this is the cross-DB prompt-hash anchor, Tier-1 audit data, and the str test must precede _SHA256_HEX_PATTERN.fullmatch, which raises a bare TypeError on a non-str and would lose the named-field diagnostic. Invalidated if: the body is inlined back into Call.__post_init__ over self.resolved_prompt_template_hash (the exemption then covers it and this entry must be deleted, not renewed), or if the repository write path stops calling it, at which point the two-caller justification for the hoist is gone.
contracts/diversion.py:R5:SinkWriteResul: R5 `not isinstance(d, RowDiversion)` inside SinkWriteResult.__post_init__. This site IS in the exempt frame — frozen dataclass, __post_init__, element-wise validation of a declared field — and the two sibling guards above it (isinstance(self.artifact, ArtifactDescriptor), isinstance(self.diversions, tuple)) are correctly exempted and do not appear in the corpus. It is flagged for a purely syntactic reason: the subject `d` is bound by `for i, d in enumerate(self.diversions)`, and _post_init_self_field_aliases_before only tracks a loop variable when the target is an ast.Name and the iterable is self.<field>, a prior alias, or a module-private call over one. Here the target is an ast.Tuple and the iterable is a call to the public builtin enumerate, so `d` is not recognised as an element of self.diversions. The index is needed for that message, which is why enumerate is here — rewriting the loop to `for d in self.diversions` purely to reach the exemption would be exactly the fingerprint-shaping churn AGENTS.md forbids. contracts/header_modes.py:R5:parse_heade: R5 `isinstance(config, dict)` in parse_header_mode. This is discriminated-union narrowing on a declared three-way parameter type `str | dict[str, str] | None`, not a defensive type check: the dict arm IS the CUSTOM mode selector — supplying a mapping is how an operator asks for explicit normalized_name -> display_name handover names, while the str arm names a built-in mode and None defaults to NORMALIZED. Every caller passes a sink config field (plugins/infrastructure/config_base.py:678, plugins/sinks/aws_s3_sink.py:215, plugins/sinks/azure_blob_sink.py:258 all pass self.headers). The value is operator-authored settings YAML that has already been loaded and shape-checked upstream, so this is Tier 1/2 config interpretation, not a Tier-3 parse of untrusted bytes — a @trust_boundary here would be a false claim about where the data came from. Nothing is silently accepted: an empty dict raises ValueError (an incomplete CUSTOM mapping would drop columns from a handover file), and any unrecognised string falls through to the final `raise ValueError(f"Invalid header mode ...")`, so there is no fall-through arm to fix. Invalidated if: the CUSTOM mapping is given its own settings field or model so the parameter collapses to `str | None`, or if sink config is parsed into a typed object before reaching this function.
contracts/secret_scrub.py:R5:_scrub_valu: R5 `isinstance(value, Mapping)` — the first arm of the recursive audit redaction walker _scrub_value. The parameter is `Any` intrinsically: the payload is an arbitrary nested structure assembled from plugin and provider data on its way into the audit trail, so there is no owned type to isinstance against, and dispatch on container semantics is the whole mechanism. This arm must be FIRST and must test Mapping (the abc, not dict): a mapping is the only shape that carries key NAMES, and key-name redaction via _is_secret_key_name is the primary control — the rebuilt comprehension is what passes each key down as parent_key so the next level can redact on name alone, before any value pattern is consulted. Testing dict instead would leak every secret held in a non-dict Mapping (a provider response wrapper, a MappingProxyType). Invalidated if: audit payloads are narrowed to an owned typed record built at the persist boundary, at which point the walker's Any and this dispatch both go away.

R5 `isinstance(value, str)` in _scrub_value — the leaf arm that inspects VALUES rather than key names. Its position between the Mapping arm and the sequence arm is load-bearing in both directions: str is itself a Sequence, so if the (list, tuple) arm were reached first every string would be walked character by character, and each character rescanned against _PATTERNS — meaning no whole-string replacement would ever fire. Why the check is right: a str is the only leaf that can carry a secret in its own body (a bearer token, a URL with credentials in the netloc), and on a hit the WHOLE string is replaced, deliberately — the inline comment states that partial redaction leaks structure. Non-str scalars (int, float, bool, None, datetime) fall through to the final `return value` unchanged, which is the intended identity for values that cannot hold a secret, not a missed dispatch arm. Invalidated if: a non-str scalar type becomes capable of carrying a credential (e.g. a secret wrapper object enters audit payloads), which would need its own arm rather than the identity default.

R5 `isinstance(value, (list, tuple))` in _scrub_value — the ordered-sequence arm. It recurses with parent_key=None, and that is the point of having a separate arm: a positional element inherits no key name from its container, so it must be judged on its own value by the str arm and can never be redacted by name. The concrete (list, tuple) pair is deliberate rather than the Sequence abc — Sequence would swallow str and bytes and destroy the whole-string replacement above. Both are rebuilt as a list because audit payloads are JSON-serialised on persist, where list and tuple are indistinguishable, so preserving the input's exact sequence type would be false precision. Invalidated if: audit payloads stop being JSON-serialised (tuple/list would then be a distinction worth preserving), or if a sequence element gains an inherited name that ought to drive key-based redaction.

R5 `isinstance(value, Set)` in _scrub_value — the unordered-collection arm, and the only one whose body exists for determinism rather than redaction. A set has no iteration order that survives a process restart (str hashing is salted), so scrubbed members are emitted `sorted(..., key=repr)`: without that, two audit writes of the same payload would serialise to different byte sequences and any hash or diff over the persisted payload would report a spurious change. `key=repr` is used because the members are arbitrary post-scrub values with no common ordering. Set is the collections.abc form so frozenset and set both land here, and it must follow the (list, tuple) arm since neither is a Set. Invalidated if: audit payloads stop admitting sets, or if deterministic ordering moves into the canonical serializer, at which point this arm should collapse into the sequence arm.

testing/__init__.py:R5:make_success_mult: R5 `isinstance(r, dict)` in the shared-contract build loop of make_success_multi, over the declared element union `dict[str, Any] | PipelineRow`. TransformResult.success_multi requires every row to share one SchemaContract INSTANCE, and when no contract is supplied this loop synthesises it from the union of all dict rows' keys. Narrowing was attempted and reverted, which is why this is J and not F: this factory's one live caller passes dicts, but rewriting the parameter as the bare `list[dict[str, Any]]` trips the check-contracts gate ('make_success_multi - rows (list)' under dict[str, Any] violations) — a form the union escapes. R5 `isinstance(r, dict)` in the row-lift comprehension of make_success_multi — the same element union as the contract loop above, but deciding something different: which rows must be CONVERTED. tui/screens/explain_screen.py:R5:Explain: R5 `isinstance(state, NodeStateOpen)` in _add_execution_state — the first of four ordered arms projecting the NodeState union into a NodeStateInfo display dict. It runs AFTER the fields common to every arm (state_id, token_id, status, input_hash, started_at) are written and returns immediately, because an open state has no completion timestamp, no duration and no output: this early return is what lets the following block read state.completed_at and state.duration_ms unguarded. Order matters — the union is projected widest-first, each arm returning once its arm-specific fields are added. Invalidated if: NodeStateOpen gains completion fields, which would make this early return drop data rather than protect the block below it.

R5 `isinstance(state, NodeStatePending)` in _add_execution_state — the second arm, positioned after the completion block (completed_at, duration_ms, context_after_json) but BEFORE the output_hash block. That placement is the whole content of the arm: a pending state has finished timing and may carry a context, but its output does not exist yet, so returning here is what keeps an absent output_hash out of the panel instead of rendering it as empty. Narrowing against our own concrete audit dataclass, per ADR-032. Invalidated if: pending states start carrying an output hash, or the panel's field order changes such that the return no longer sits between the two blocks it separates.

R5 `isinstance(state, NodeStateCompleted)` in _add_execution_state — the third arm, and the first that adds a field no other arm has: success_reason_json, the structured record of WHY a transform succeeded (the 'action' the plugin reported). It is emitted only when non-None, since a completed state need not carry a reason, and the arm returns so the failure arm below cannot also fire. Reached only after Open and Pending have returned, so the state here is known to have both a completion time and an output. Invalidated if: success_reason_json moves to a shared base, or completed and failed states are merged into one arm with an outcome discriminator field.

R5 `isinstance(state, NodeStateFailed)` in _add_execution_state — the fourth and final arm, adding error_json. Its significance is what follows it: the function ends in `raise TypeError(f"Unsupported node state type: {type(state).__name__}")`, so this chain has NO silent fall-through — a fifth NodeState arm added upstream fails loudly here instead of quietly rendering a detail panel missing the operator's error payload. That terminal raise is the reason each arm can safely be a narrow isinstance rather than a defensive hasattr probe. Invalidated if: the terminal raise is softened to a return or a log (the chain would then need exhaustiveness enforced some other way before this entry could be renewed).

R5 `isinstance(state, (NodeStatePending, NodeStateCompleted, NodeStateFailed))` inside the max() key lambda in _select_node_state_for_display. NodeState (contracts/audit.py:401) is the closed union NodeStateOpen | NodeStatePending | NodeStateCompleted | NodeStateFailed, and only the latter three declare completed_at — NodeStateOpen has started_at alone. The isinstance is therefore an attribute-presence discriminator that keeps the sort key TOTAL: without it, choosing 'the most recent state' either crashes with AttributeError on an in-flight node or has to fall back to a getattr probe, which the whole-tree gate rightly forbids. Picking the wrong state here is not cosmetic: it is the row the operator reads as the node's outcome. Grouping the three arms in one tuple is exact, not lazy — they are precisely the arms that reached a completion timestamp. Invalidated if: NodeStateOpen gains completed_at (the union then has a uniform key and the isinstance goes), or a fifth arm is added without it — a parity sweep this entry should force.

R5 `not isinstance(self._state, UninitializedState)` in ExplainScreen.load — a state-machine transition PRECONDITION, not a data type check. load() is documented as the single legal UninitializedState -> LoadedState|LoadingFailedState edge, and this is the runtime enforcement of that edge: on violation it raises InvalidStateTransitionError carrying the method, the current state name and the allowed set, which is what makes 'call clear() first' actionable to a caller. Because ScreenState is a union of three distinct classes rather than one class with a tag field, the state's TYPE is its discriminator — isinstance is the only way to ask which state we are in. Allowing a second load would silently discard an already-loaded run's caches. Invalidated if: the screen adopts an explicit state tag (enum field) or a state-machine helper, so transitions are checked against a declared table rather than by type.

R5 `isinstance(self._state, LoadedState)` in ExplainScreen.on_tree_select. ScreenState (explain_screen.py:97) is a closed discriminated union of three frozen dataclasses — UninitializedState | LoadingFailedState | LoadedState — and this narrowing is what makes the arm's body type-safe: LoadedState is the only arm carrying focused_state_by_node_id and latest_state_by_node_id, the caches the very next line reads, as well as the db/run_id the load call needs. Invalidated if: ScreenState gains a fourth arm that also carries the per-node caches, or the caches move onto a shared base class — either would make this test too narrow rather than merely unnecessary.

R5 `isinstance(self._state, LoadingFailedState)` in ExplainScreen.on_tree_select — the second arm of the same ScreenState narrowing, reached only when the state is not LoadedState. It is not a duplicate of the LoadedState arm and not dead: LoadingFailedState deliberately preserves db and run_id after a failed structural load, so a node the operator selects can still be looked up LIVE (no cache exists, so _load_node_state runs with its default scan_for_state=True). Dropping this arm would turn a recoverable database hiccup into a permanently blank detail panel. Anything else — i.e. UninitializedState — falls through to update_state(None), which is the honest 'nothing selected' rendering, not a swallowed error. Invalidated if: LoadingFailedState stops carrying db/run_id, at which point there is nothing to look up and the arm should be deleted rather than justified.

R5 `isinstance(self._state, LoadedState)` in ExplainScreen.render — the same ScreenState narrowing as on_tree_select but selecting a different capability: LoadedState is the only arm carrying `.tree`, so this is the test that decides whether a lineage tree section can be rendered at all. The other two arms render their own sections (the run id line above comes from _get_run_id, which pattern-matches the union separately), so this is a section gate, not an error check, and there is nothing to raise. Invalidated if: the tree moves onto ScreenState generally, or render() is restructured to a single `match self._state` over the union like _get_run_id already uses.

R5 `not isinstance(self._state, LoadingFailedState)` in ExplainScreen.retry — the mirror precondition to load(), and it names a different reason: LoadingFailedState is the ONLY arm that preserves the db handle and run_id needed to attempt the load again (the inline comment says so), so retry from any other state has no inputs and could only fabricate them. It raises the same InvalidStateTransitionError with its own allowed set, keeping the documented transition table enforceable rather than advisory.
